cover.headline: India's replacement-tyre leader in a raw-material squeeze, with Europe finally being fixed: cheap on normal earnings
cover.lead: Apollo Tyres makes truck, car, farm and two-wheeler tyres in India (~69% of revenue) and, as Apollo Vredestein, premium car and farm tyres for Europe (~26%). Q1FY27 showed both sides of the story: India volume up ~12% and revenue +15.6%, but raw materials +17% q/q cut the consolidated EBITDA margin to 11.7%, and Europe earned 8.9% while the Enschede plant (Netherlands) was shut. We forecast EPS of ₹27.0 / ₹34.3 / ₹40.2 for FY27-29E, close to the street. The street values Apollo on **P/E on one-year-forward EPS** (MOSL 16x FY28E, Emkay 18x Jun-28E; ICICI Direct uses 7x EV/EBITDA). The house rule (its forward P/E median since 2021 on EPS before one-offs, 16.0x, cut by the 10.5% tyre-sector de-rating) gives **14.5x Sep-28E EPS of ₹37.2 = {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): we initiate with BUY**. Cross-checks: DCF ₹590; EV/EBITDA ₹426, below the price. Bull case {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}; bear case {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}.

arguments.h: India is growing faster than the industry and gaining share
arguments.p: Standalone revenue grew 15.6% in Q1FY27, the fastest in 14 quarters, with double-digit volume in replacement, OEM and exports; management estimates its TBR replacement share back above 30% and PCR at 21%+. Capacity runs in the 90s and a ₹5,800 cr Andhra Pradesh expansion (+17-20% India capacity) starts at end-FY27. We model APMEA revenue +15% / +11% / +10% for FY27-29E.

arguments.h: The margin squeeze is a lag, not a reset
arguments.p: Raw materials rose ~17% in Q1 and ~8% more in Q2 (rubber ₹225 to ₹260+/kg). Apollo had taken ~11% of the 15-16% price increases needed by early August, competitors followed, and OEM formula prices catch up with a quarter's lag; CRISIL sees industry margins at 11.5-12% in FY27 and 13-13.5% in FY28. We assume {{F.ebitdaMargin.0|pct}} for FY27E and {{F.ebitdaMargin.2|pct}} by FY29E, below the FY24 peak (17.6%).

arguments.h: Europe: the expensive part is done
arguments.p: Enschede stopped production in Jun-2026 after ₹1,128 cr of charges in FY25-26; volumes move to Hungary, India and offtake partners. Management says Europe would have earned ~11% in Q1 without overlap costs and targets "high teens". We assume 12% / 14% / 15% segment margins for FY27-29E (13.0% in FY26), still below the 16% the company calls normal. ~EUR55 mn of cash costs fall in FY27.

At ₹405 Apollo trades at 11.8x our FY28E and 10.9x Sep-28E EPS, against a 16.0x median since 2021 on EPS before one-offs; the stock is 26% below its all-time high and 22% below its 52-week high. Even after the 10.5% sector de-rating, 14.5x gives {{dcf.tp|inr}}, close to the post-Q1 street median (₹528). The risk is the capex cycle: FY27-28E free cash flow is thin and net debt rises.

catalysts: Q2FY27 results (due by mid-November 2026): the size of the second raw-material step-up (~8% q/q) against ~11% of price increases and OEM pass-through.
Natural rubber after the monsoon: management expects it to cool from Q3FY27; Apollo buys about half its rubber abroad and domestic prices track import parity.
Europe in H2FY27: the first quarters without Enschede's costs, the Hungary PCR ramp-up (17,000 to 21,000 tyres a day) and the agri offtake stabilising.
Andhra Pradesh capacity from end-FY27 and FY28 capex (possibly above ₹3,000 cr): returns on the ₹5,800 cr plan.
A new CFO after Gaurav Kumar's resignation (Aug-2026), and the 2026-31 strategy targets management said it would set out.

sections.title: An Indian truck- and car-tyre leader with a premium European brand on the side

blocks.p: Apollo Tyres sells tyres for trucks and buses, passenger cars and SUVs, light trucks, tractors and farm machines, two-wheelers and off-highway vehicles. In Q1FY27 consolidated revenue was 69% India, 26% Europe and 5% other markets; truck and bus tyres 41%, passenger vehicles 36%, farm and off-highway 11%, light trucks 7%; 79% went to the replacement market and 21% to vehicle makers. In India (standalone) the mix is heavier in trucks: truck and bus 53%, passenger vehicles 22%; replacement 66%, OEM 23%, exports 11%. Management estimates its replacement share at 30%+ in truck radials (TBR) and 21%+ in car radials (PCR).

It makes tyres in five Indian plants (Perambra and Kalamassery in Kerala, Limda in Gujarat, Chennai, and Chinnapandur in Andhra Pradesh) and at Gyöngyöshalász in Hungary; the Enschede plant in the Netherlands, home of the Vredestein brand, stopped production in Jun-2026 and remains an R&D site. India runs at ~91% utilisation and Europe at ~94% (Q1FY27). Apollo reports three segments: **APMEA** (India plus small units in the UAE, Thailand, Malaysia and South Africa), **Europe** (Apollo Vredestein and the ReifenCom distribution business in Germany) and **Others** (Americas sales and corporate entities).

sections.title: From a Kerala truck-tyre maker to a two-continent group; the last decade was about digesting Europe and big plants

blocks.p: Apollo Tyres was incorporated in Kerala in 1972 (CIN) and is run by the Kanwar family (Chairman Onkar Kanwar, Vice Chairman & MD Neeraj Kanwar). It became a two-continent group through Europe (the Vredestein brand and the Enschede plant in the Netherlands, then a greenfield plant in Hungary). The FY17-21 build-out of Hungary and Andhra Pradesh, funded partly with equity (FY18, FY21), drove borrowings to ₹7,334 cr and ROE to 3-9%. FY22-26 were years of small capex and deleveraging. Since FY25 the agenda has been fixing Europe's cost base (closing Enschede) and, from FY27, adding capacity in India again. Share count: 63.51 cr shares of ₹1 since FY21 (no change in FY25 or FY26).

sections.title: Indian tyres: steady volume, a raw-material squeeze in FY27, a capex wave; Europe flat

blocks.p: Indian tyre industry revenue ~₹1.36 lakh cr in FY26; the top six makers are ~85% of it (CRISIL, 24-Aug-2026). Demand follows the vehicle parc and freight (replacement), new vehicle sales (OEM) and exports. After 7-8% volume growth in FY26, helped by the GST cut on tyres, CRISIL (24-Aug-2026) expects 4-5% in FY27, with key inputs up 35-40% and operating margins down 200-250 bp to ~11.5-12%, recovering to 13-13.5% in FY28 if costs stabilise: "a cost-pass-through lag rather than a structural profitability reset". The top six makers plan ~₹18,000 cr of capex in FY27-28, nearly double the previous two years; Apollo's ₹5,800 cr AP plan is part of that wave.

bullets: **Raw materials.** Kottayam RSS-4 ₹27,300 per quintal (₹273/kg) on 3-Sep-2026; global futures ~240 US cents/kg on 1-Sep-2026, near the highest since 2013 (Procurement Resource, 10-Sep-2026). Apollo's own basket: rubber ~₹200/kg in Q4FY26, ~₹225 in Q1FY27, ₹260+ expected in Q2FY27. Natural rubber, synthetic rubber, carbon black and steel cord make up most of the cost; ~50% of Apollo's raw materials are imported, so a weaker rupee adds to the bill (7-8% in Q1FY27, CFO).

**Pricing.** Industry took 7-9% of price increases by Q1FY27 with more planned in Q2 (CLSA via Moneycontrol, 12-Aug-2026); Apollo ~11% by early August, 15-16% needed; competitors followed with similar magnitude (CFO, 7-Aug-2026). Replacement prices move first; OEM contracts follow with a quarter's lag through formulas or negotiation.

**Europe.** European replacement market flat to negative for two years (CFO, May-2026); EU anti-dumping duties on Chinese tyres announced in 2026 help mid-tier brands (Q1FY27 call); Apollo is a price follower in Europe given its size; Europe needs smaller price increases for the same raw-material rise because natural rubber is a smaller share.

**Regulation and imports.** AIS-142 phase 2 noise norms from H2FY27 push truck OEMs towards radials; DGFT licensing of tyre imports since Jun-2020 limits Chinese imports (CARE); GST cut on tyres (Sep-2025) lifted replacement demand.

**Competition.** MRF, Apollo, CEAT and JK Tyre lead in India (MRF and Apollo are the two largest in truck tyres, CFO); BKT is entering truck and car radials. In Europe Apollo competes with Michelin, Continental, Goodyear, Bridgestone, Pirelli and Asian imports, and is a price follower.

blocks.callout: **Verdict:** the Indian tailwind reaches Apollo in full: it has the brands, dealers and truck-radial share to grow with the market, and it is adding capacity at the right time. What it cannot escape is the raw-material cycle; FY27 margins depend on how fast rubber falls. Europe is a self-help story, not a market tailwind.

sections.title: India: share gains, full plants and a raw-material squeeze; margins should recover with a lag

blocks.p: APMEA external revenue grew from ₹11,061 cr (FY20) to ₹19,039 cr (FY26). The India business (standalone) did ₹19,816 cr in FY26 (+9.0%) at a 14.5% EBITDA margin (12.1% in FY25), and accelerated through the year on the GST cut and the BCCI sponsorship: +13.2% in Q3FY26, +14.3% in Q4 and +15.6% in Q1FY27, with volume up ~12% (replacement +13%, OEM +10%, exports +15%). The margin fell to 12% in Q1FY27 (13.6%) as raw materials rose ~17% q/q: natural rubber ~₹225/kg, synthetic rubber ₹250, carbon black ₹125, steel cord ₹165. Apollo cut advertising ~50% after the Q4 jersey activation to defend it.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** we model APMEA revenue +15% / +11% / +10% for FY27-29E and a segment margin of 14.2% / 15% / 15.3% (FY26 16.2%; FY20-26 average ~15%). That assumes standalone margins of ~12% in H1FY27, ~13.5% in H2 and 13.5-14% in FY28-29: a recovery with a lag, as in FY23-24, but not to the FY24 peak. The extra capacity from Andhra Pradesh (+10,500 PCR and +3,600 TBR tyres a day) matters for FY28-29 volume; until then growth is capped by utilisation in the 90s.

sections.title: Europe: flat sales, a high-cost plant closed, and a margin target the company has missed for years

blocks.p: Europe was ₹8,371 cr of external revenue in FY26 (29% of the group), of which the manufacturing and sales business (Vredestein and Apollo brands) was EUR678 mn at a 14% EBITDA margin and ReifenCom (a German tyre distributor) EUR40-43 mn a quarter at a 2-3% margin (Q4FY26, Q1FY27). In euros the business has been flat for two years (EUR674 mn in FY25, EUR678 mn in FY26): the European replacement market has been "flattish to negative", while Dutch wages rose 12-13% over two to three years and energy stayed expensive (CFO, May-2026). The margin slid from 16%+ ("our earlier normal") to 14-15% in FY25-26 and 8.9% in Q1FY27. Premium mix is high: ultra-high-performance tyres were 50-52% of Europe's mix in Q3-Q4FY26.

blocks.title: Moat scorecard
blocks.source: GAM research compilation (annual reports, presentations and calls to Aug-2026)

blocks.callout: **Honest verdict:** Apollo has a real franchise in India: the top-two position in truck radials, a strong replacement brand and dealer network, and scale that lets it add capacity when demand is there. That is a moat against new entrants, not against the cycle: it earns industry margins that rise and fall with rubber, and it has no cost advantage over MRF, CEAT or JK. Europe has a good brand (Vredestein) but has not earned a good return; the closure is an admission of that.

sections.title: Revenue up 74% in six years; profit has swung with rubber, Europe and one-offs

blocks.p: Apollo's revenue was ₹16,350 cr in FY20 and ₹28,471 cr in FY26 (9.7% a year), almost all of it from India: the APMEA segment grew from ₹11,061 cr to ₹19,039 cr while Europe went from ₹5,165 cr to ₹8,371 cr, helped by a weaker rupee. Profit has been far more volatile. The EBITDA margin swung between 11% and 18% since FY18 with natural rubber and crude, and reported profit carries large one-offs: ₹608 cr of exceptional charges in FY21 (Europe), ₹169 cr in FY25 and ₹1,034 cr in FY26 (the Enschede closure), plus a ~₹570 cr deferred-tax write-back in FY26. Before one-offs EPS was ₹10.4 in FY21, ₹29.3 at the FY24 peak, ₹19.6 in FY25 and ₹26.7 in FY26 (MOSL basis); reported EPS was ₹21.6.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** Apollo is a cyclical business with a structural problem it has finally addressed. The India business earns a normal tyre-industry margin that moves with rubber; Europe, a quarter of revenue, has earned 13-15% EBITDA margins since FY24 on a high-cost Dutch plant, and its restructuring has cost ₹1,128 cr of charges in FY25-26. Read reported EPS with care: FY26's ₹21.6 is depressed by the closure and flattered by a tax write-back; ₹26.7 is the cleaner number.

The operating picture is a margin squeeze: EBITDA flat on revenue +13%. Q2 brings ~8% more raw-material inflation against 3-4% of extra price; our FY27E EBITDA margin of {{F.ebitdaMargin.0|pct}} assumes ~12% in Q2 and ~13.5-14.5% in H2 as price increases, OEM pass-through, lower rubber and Enschede savings arrive.

sections.title: Five years of small capex repaired the balance sheet; a ₹5,800 cr expansion starts now

blocks.p: Apollo spent heavily in FY17-20 (Hungary and the Andhra Pradesh greenfield: ₹11,550 cr of capex in four years) and borrowings rose to ₹7,334 cr. Then it switched to "bite-sized" capex: ₹5,525 cr in FY22-26, below depreciation in most years, against ₹13,221 cr of operating cash. Borrowings (incl. leases) fell to ₹3,675 cr and net debt to EBITDA from 3.2x (Mar-2020) to 0.4x (Mar-2026). ROCE recovered to 11-16% in FY24-26 (Screener basis; company 13.4% in FY26), still short of the company's 15% target. The cycle has turned: utilisation is in the 90s and the board approved ₹5,800 cr for Andhra Pradesh over FY27-29 (+17-18% India PCR and +20% TBR capacity) on top of a Hungary PCR expansion. FY27 capex is guided at ₹3,000-3,500 cr, two to three times FY26.

blocks.callout: **The capital question:** the last time Apollo built big (FY17-21) ROE fell to 3-9% for five years. This time the plan is in its home market, where demand is outrunning capacity, at ~₹17 cr per tonne a day, and the balance sheet starts at 0.4x net debt to EBITDA. We model net debt rising to ~₹3,000 cr (incl. leases) in FY27-28E before falling, and ROE of {{F.roe.0|pct}} / {{F.roe.1|pct}} / {{F.roe.2|pct}} for FY27-29E: adequate, not exciting.

sections.title: Earnings quality: real cash, but every year since FY24 has carried one-offs

bullets: **Cash conversion is strong.** Cash from operations was ₹3,667 cr in FY26 against EBITDA of ₹4,170 cr (88%), and ₹8,930 cr over FY24-26. FY27E free cash flow turns negative on capex; FY27 also pays ~EUR55 mn of Enschede cash costs provided in FY26.

**Exceptional items every year.** FY24 ₹77 cr, FY25 ₹169 cr, FY26 ₹1,034 cr (Enschede ₹1,000 cr, labour codes ₹26 cr, VRS ₹7 cr), Q1FY27 a ₹23.5 cr gain. Screener nets them into "other income" (FY26: −₹900 cr), so its EPS history is noisy. We use EPS before one-offs (MOSL basis) for the valuation history and forecast none.
**A tax write-back flatters FY26.** Moving to the 25% regime wrote back ~₹570 cr of deferred tax in Q4FY26; reported FY26 tax was −5% and EPS ₹21.6 (₹26.7 before one-offs on MOSL's basis).

**Other income is small but mixed.** FY26 ₹133.4 cr: interest ₹37.2 cr, FX gains ₹65.6 cr, asset-sale gains ₹19.3 cr, other ₹11.3 cr. We forecast ₹{{F.otherIncome.0|num}} / {{F.otherIncome.1|num}} / {{F.otherIncome.2|num}} cr.

**Europe's other operating income is falling.** Hungary state aid was amortised over ten years; as TBR assets moved to India part of it had to be reversed (−2pp of Europe revenue growth in Q4FY26). Non-cash, but it lowers reported Europe revenue and margin for a few quarters.

**Impairment judgement.** The Enschede impairment used fair value less costs of disposal (Level 3, independent valuer); some plant expected to be redeployed was not impaired. Goodwill ₹277 cr at Mar-26.

blocks.callout: **Accounting flag: AMBER.** Clean audit (S.R. Batliboi), strong cash conversion, but recurring "exceptional" items (Europe restructuring in FY21, FY25 and FY26), a large tax write-back and FX gains in other income make reported EPS a poor guide. Investors should use profit before one-offs and watch FY27 cash flow for the closure payments.

sections.title: Net debt of ₹1,532 cr at Mar-26 (₹2,569 cr with leases): the strongest in a decade

blocks.p: At Mar-2026 Apollo had ₹2,632 cr of bank borrowings and debentures and ₹1,044 cr of lease liabilities against ₹1,044 cr of cash: net debt of ₹1,532 cr before leases (the company says ~₹1,600 cr, 0.4x EBITDA) and ~₹1,700 cr at Jun-26. Two items to watch: current provisions jumped to ₹854 cr (₹289 cr) mostly for the Enschede social plan, ~EUR55 mn+ of which is paid in cash in FY27 (not in our P&L, as it was provided in FY26); and deferred tax liabilities of ₹1,455 cr fell by ~₹340 cr after the move to the 25% tax regime. Working capital is moderate: ~128 days of inventory, ~41 of receivables and ~76 of payables (Screener).

sections.title: The street after Q1: mostly Buy, targets ₹460-590, median ₹528

blocks.p: After the Q1FY27 results (7-Aug-2026) Motilal Oswal kept Buy with ₹528 (16x FY28E EPS), expecting margins to revive fully in FY28 on normal costs and Europe's restructuring; Emkay kept Buy and raised its target to ₹575 (18x Jun-28E EPS) on pricing power; ICICI Direct kept Buy at ₹510 (7x FY28E EV/EBITDA; its text also cites ₹425); ICICI Securities had Buy at ₹530; Nomura stayed Neutral (₹468) on margin and capex risk; JPMorgan Neutral at ₹460; UBS upgraded to Buy at ₹590 (23-Aug-2026). Median of the seven post-Q1 targets: ₹528, +30% vs the 30-Sep-2026 close of ₹405. The two houses that publish full models value Apollo on **P/E on one-year-forward EPS**; EV/EBITDA (6.3-7x FY28E) is the other method in use. Some notes value India and Europe separately; none we read did so on or before 30-Sep-2026.

sections.title: Our honest summary: a cyclical leader at a cyclical low; BUY

blocks.callout: **What you are buying:** one of India's two largest truck-tyre makers, growing faster than the market with a strong replacement brand, plus a European business that has under-earned for years and has just shut its highest-cost plant. Earnings are at a cyclical low: raw materials are up ~25% in two quarters and price increases lag; Europe is mid-restructuring. Capex triples in FY27-28 for new Indian capacity, so free cash flow is thin and net debt rises for two years.

**What you are paying:** 15.0x our FY27E and 11.8x FY28E EPS. Apollo's own forward P/E on EPS before one-offs has a median of 16.0x since 2021; Indian tyre stocks were 10.5% below their five-year medians on 30-Sep-2026, which gives 14.5x Sep-28E EPS and {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): BUY on our rule. The DCF (₹590) supports it; EV/EBITDA (₹426) does not, because it leans hardest on the margin recovery.

assumptions._note: GAM Research forecast drivers for Apollo Tyres Ltd (consolidated, Rs crore). FY26 (Mar-2026) is the last reported year; Q1FY27 (Jun-2026, reported 7-Aug-2026) is the last quarter known on 30-Sep-2026. Segment model on the company's three reported geographic segments (external revenue; segment EBITDA = segment result + depreciation, which includes the other income allocated to segments). Consolidated EBITDA = sum of segments less that other income (the 'unallocated' line), which is then added back below EBITDA as other income. No minorities (EPS = profit / 63.51 cr shares).

segments.name: APMEA (India-led)
segments._why: FY27E +15%: standalone (India) revenue +15.6% in Q1FY27 (volume ~+12%: replacement +13%, OEM +10%, exports +15%) and only 3-4% of the 7-9% Q1 price increases flowed into Q1 revenue; ~11% of increases taken by early August with 1-2% in July and ~2% in August, and OEM formula pass-through from Q2 (Q1FY27 call, 7-Aug-2026). Capacity utilisation is in the 90s, so H2 volume growth slows against a GST-boosted base (Q3FY26 +13%, Q4FY26 +14%). FY28E +11%: the Andhra Pradesh expansion (+10,500 PCR and +3,600 TBR tyres a day, ~17-20% more India capacity) starts at end-FY27 and ramps through FY28; price carry-over. FY29E +10%. MOSL standalone FY27E +10.5%; Emkay consolidated +15%.
segments._revWhy: Driver is external revenue itself (after inter-segment sales to Europe).
segments._marginWhy: Segment EBITDA (incl. allocated other income) on external revenue: 16.2% in FY26, 13.4% in FY25, 19.2% in FY24 (FY20-26 median 13.4%, mean 14.9%). It runs ~1.5 pt above standalone EBITDA margin (14.5% in FY26) because export margins earned on inter-segment sales stay in APMEA. Q1FY27 standalone margin 12.0% (13.6%) with raw materials +17% q/q and a further +8% expected in Q2; natural rubber ~Rs225/kg in Q1, ~Rs260+ in Q2, expected to cool from Q3. FY27E 14.2% (standalone ~12.6%: H1 ~12%, H2 ~13.5%); FY28E 15.0% and FY29E 15.3% (standalone ~13.5-14%), back near the FY20-26 average, not the FY24 peak. CRISIL (24-Aug-2026): industry margin 11.5-12% in FY27, 13-13.5% in FY28.

segments.name: Europe (Vredestein, ReifenCom)
segments._why: FY27E +8%: in euros Europe manufacturing revenue was flat in Q1FY27 (EUR147 mn, +0.5%) with low-single-digit volume growth (PCR replacement double-digit; agri tyres down as Enschede closed, 20-25% of agri now bought from offtake partners), but the euro averaged ~10% more in rupees (MOSL: Europe revenue +10.3% in INR terms). We assume ~+2% in euros and ~+6% from the euro's rupee value over the year. FY28E +7%: Hungary PCR capacity 17,000 to 21,000 tyres a day from H2FY27, EU anti-dumping duties on Chinese tyres help the Apollo brand at the lower end (call), ~4% FX/price. FY29E +6%. ReifenCom (distribution, EUR40-43 mn a quarter at 2-3% EBITDA) is inside this segment.
segments._revWhy: Driver is external revenue itself (in rupees).
segments._marginWhy: Segment EBITDA margin 13.0% in FY26, 13.6% in FY25, 15.2% in FY24 (FY22-26 average 14.3%); company basis (excl. ReifenCom) 14.0% in FY26 and 8.9% in Q1FY27, ~11% without the Enschede/Hungary cost overlap (CFO). Enschede stopped production in Jun-2026; benefits from H2FY27 (management); 'high teens' is the full-year aspiration once the footprint is right. FY27E 12.0% (H1 ~9.5%, H2 ~14%); FY28E 14.0%; FY29E 15.0%: below management's high-teens aim because Europe raw materials lag (only 3-4% of a needed ~10% price increase taken by Aug-2026) and the market is flat.

segments.name: Others (Americas, corporate)
segments._why: Americas sales (US weak: dealer inventories not clearing, Q1FY27 call) and corporate entities; 4% of revenue.
segments._marginWhy: Segment EBITDA 10.1% of external revenue in FY26 (FY23-25: 21-30%, swollen by corporate income and inter-segment margins that are not stable). We hold 10%.

assumptions._unallocLabel: Other income included in segment results (moved below EBITDA)
assumptions._unallocWhy: Segment results include other income (FY26 Rs133 cr: segment EBITDA Rs4,277 cr vs company EBITDA Rs4,143 cr). We take it out of EBITDA here and add the same amount back as other income below, so reported EBITDA and PBT are not double counted.
assumptions._capexWhy: Guidance: ~Rs3,000-3,500 cr in FY27 (Q4FY26 call, May-2026: Rs3,500 cr, ~Rs3,000 cr of it in India; MOSL after Q1: ~Rs3,000 cr reiterated); Q1FY27 Rs650 cr. The board approved Rs5,800 cr for the Andhra Pradesh plant over FY27-29 (Feb-2026: +10,500 PCR and +3,600 TBR tyres a day at ~Rs17 cr per tonne-day); FY28 'might be even higher than Rs3,000 cr', FY29 tapering (Q3FY26 call). Maintenance ~Rs700 cr a year. FY26 cash capex Rs1,355 cr (Screener investing cash flow basis).
assumptions._depWhy: FY26 depreciation Rs1,543 cr (incl. right-of-use assets) = 4.75% of average gross block (Rs32,508 cr, Screener basis, FY25-26); Q1FY27 Rs391 cr (Rs1,564 cr annualised). The engine depreciates new capex at once and holds CWIP (Rs1,077 cr at Mar-26, up from Rs435 cr) flat, while much of the AP capex is CWIP until end-FY27; 4.6% offsets that timing. FY27E Rs1,638 cr vs MOSL Rs1,615 cr.
assumptions._treasuryWhy: Apollo has net debt (Rs3,675 cr of borrowings incl. Rs1,044 cr of leases vs Rs1,044 cr of cash at Mar-26), so the engine's treasury is negative and earns nothing; interest on the ~Rs1,000 cr of cash is inside other income below.
assumptions._otherIncomeWhy: Built from FY26 note B24 (Rs133 cr): interest on bank deposits Rs14 cr and other interest (incl. on a government grant) Rs23 cr, foreign-exchange gains Rs66 cr, profit on asset sales Rs19 cr, miscellaneous Rs10 cr, investment income Rs1 cr. Recurring core ~Rs50 cr (interest and misc.); FX gains recur while the rupee weakens. FY27E Rs125 cr = Q1 Rs58 cr (company basis, before the Rs23.5 cr exceptional gain that Screener adds) + ~Rs22 cr a quarter (MOSL: Rs21-23 cr a quarter). FY28-29E ~Rs110-115 cr. TTM-Jun-26 on the company basis Rs148 cr.
assumptions._interestWhy: FY26 finance costs Rs391 cr (AR; Screener Rs419 cr) after borrowings fell from Rs2,977 cr to Rs2,632 cr (ex-leases); Q1FY27 Rs92 cr. Capex of Rs6,500 cr over FY27-28 against ~Rs4,000 cr of operating cash means borrowing again ('we will be a net borrower', CFO): +Rs40 cr in FY27E and +Rs50 cr more in FY28E. MOSL FY27E Rs435 cr.
assumptions._taxWhy: India moved to the 25.2% regime from FY27 (Finance Act 2026); Europe ~20% (Q4FY26 call). Q1FY27 25.4%. FY26 was −5% on a ~Rs570 cr deferred-tax write-back.
assumptions._payoutWhy: FY26 dividend Rs6.0 a share (interim Rs3.5, final Rs2.5) = 22% of EPS before one-offs (Rs26.7) and 28% of reported EPS; FY25 Rs5.0. Policy: at least 20% of standalone profit.

dcf._betaWhy: A cyclical, raw-material-driven margin, a European business with high fixed costs and modest net debt (~0.4x EBITDA): beta 1.0 gives a 12.5% cost of equity, used as the discount rate (debt is ~6% of market value, so WACC would be ~12.1%).
dcf._tgWhy: Indian tyre demand grows with the vehicle parc and freight plus price; Europe is flat. 5.5% nominal (house range 5-6%).
dcf._fadeGrowthWhy: Revenue growth fades from ~9% to 7.5% over 12 years: India 9-10%, Europe 3-4%.
dcf._fadeMarginWhy: EBITDA margin fades to 14.5%, near the FY20-26 median (14%) and below FY24's 17.6%.
dcf._fadeCapexWhy: Capex fades from 5.8% of revenue (FY29E) to 5.5% (FY20-26 average ~5.5%); depreciation 5.3% of revenue (FY26 5.4%).

bull.label: Bull
bull.narrative: Natural rubber falls back towards ₹200/kg from Q3FY27 while the 11-16% price increases stick (the industry's best margins come in a falling raw-material cycle, CFO); India keeps double-digit volume on the new AP capacity; Europe reaches management's mid-teens margin by FY28 as Enschede's costs go and Hungary ramps up.

bear.label: Bear
bear.narrative: Rubber and crude-linked inputs stay high and a weak monsoon and fuel prices slow truck and farm demand; price increases slip as competitors and Chinese imports undercut; Europe stays flat with agri volumes lost to the offtake transition, so the margin stays near Q1FY27's 12% and the ₹5,800 cr AP capex earns little before FY29.

methods.name: P/E
methods.why: How the street values Apollo: P/E on one-year-forward EPS (MOSL 16x FY28E, 7-Aug-2026; Emkay 18x Jun-28E, 9-Aug-2026). Multiple derived in APOLLOTYRE.ctx.js and written by APOLLOTYRE.val.js.

methods.name: EV/EBITDA
methods.why: The second street method (ICICI Direct 7x FY28E; Nomura 6.3x FY28F earlier): values the operating business and deducts net debt.

methods.name: DCF
methods.why: Tests whether cash flows support the price: 12-year FCFF, Ke 12.5%, terminal growth 5.5%, less net debt.
